title: Principia: Relational Physics Tests for Video Models
claim: Single-object motion can look plausible, but comparing paired objects under the same law exposes violations that absolute inspection misses.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right frame sequences, blue vs red boxes, dashed divider
description: Two stacked rows of four photo panels each, split by a dashed horizontal line. Each row shows a frame sequence read left to right, ending in an arrow to a final panel. The scene is two wooden ramps forming an inverted V, set against a blurred green outdoor background. Row (a) is captioned 'Single object generation: motion looks physically plausible.' One block slides down the right ramp, tracked by blue boxes. A blue arrow in the last panel shows the direction. Row (b) is captioned 'Paired object generation: arrival times do not match. Constraint t1 = t2 is violated.' Two blocks slide down opposite ramps, tracked by red boxes. In the last panel, two red arrows of different lengths show the mismatch. Blue means plausible and red means violation. The eye goes first to the colored boxes and arrows.
caption: Principia tests physical reasoning in video models through paired-object relational tests. Each panel shows a real-world experimental setup encoding a relational constraint between two objects obeying the same physical law (a-g); these constraints hold independent of camera, scale, or frame rate. We test whether modern video generators and vision-language models preserve them.
abstract: Evaluating physical reasoning in video models is difficult because absolute motion measurements depend on frame rate, object scale, and camera calibration, all of which are often ambiguous or unavailable in generated video. We propose a different approach. When two objects in the same scene obey the same physical law, their motions must satisfy predictable relationships, and these relationships hold independent of calibration. We introduce Principia, a benchmark that evaluates Newtonian physics through relational consistency between paired objects. Principia spans eight phenomena - gravity, restitution, friction, rotational inertia, projectile motion, momentum, pendulum, and mass-spring oscillation - across translational, rotational, collisional, and oscillatory dynamics, using real-world scenes recorded under controlled protocols. We also introduce a calibration-independent consistency score that quantifies physical violation directly in image space. Across thousands of generations from six state-of-the-art video generators, no model exceeds 0.42 on Principia despite all scoring around 0.8 on VBench. Vision-language models are evaluated on their ability to detect relational physics violations, with the best model achieving only 67% accuracy and most performing near chance level.
